title: Economic Stewardship in the Next American Founding
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/david-ciepley
text:
The corporation is one of the master keys to understanding the unique trajectory of Western civilization. In saying this, I mean not only the business corporation, as important as it is, but also the broader family of corporations, including churches, towns, universities, hospitals, foundations—in short, any organization that operates as a separate legal entity, owning property and making contracts in its own name. And that includes the state itself. After the Roman Catholic Church’s marriage policy undermined clan organizations, it was the corporate form of organization that filled their place.

As a genus, corporations are not about business. They are about governance. The corporation is a device for dedicating property to a purpose in perpetuity—whether that purpose be healing souls, healing bodies, providing education, building infrastructure, or brewing beer. And this is done by the public authority creating a perpetual legal entity, or “legal person,” that owns the property forever, and putting it under the control not of owners (because the legal entity is the owner) but of stewards (such as board members) with a duty to faithfully advance its purpose. In recent decades, however, the business corporation, in particular, has fallen off the wagon. Is there a way to get it back on board?

There have been three great corporate eras, in each of which a different type of corporation served as society’s lead organization.11xDavid Ciepley, “The Corporation as a Chartered Government,” Hofstra Law Review, vol. 51, no. 4 (2023), 815–877; https://scholarlycommons.law.hofstra.edu/hlr/vol51/iss4/3. The first was the medieval era of ecclesiastical corporations such as monasteries, cathedral chapters, and the earliest universities. Then, extending from the late-medieval into the early-modern period, came the era of civil corporations, such as towns and guilds. And, finally, we have the age of the business corporation, stretching from the early-modern period to the present.

This third era itself contains three successive waves of distinctive corporate formations: The first wave was that of the great trading companies, such as the British and Dutch East India companies; the second, that of the great industrial combines; and the third is today’s globalist wave of mobile, disaggregated, short-term-focused corporations—what I call “neoliberal” corporations.

I begin by surfing these three waves a bit, to help us understand how we’ve gotten to where we are and the challenges that we now face. Doing so also reveals striking connections between these corporate waves and the Founding and re-foundings of the American republic. This isn’t happenstance. For those Americans involved with the Founding of the republic, as well as those involved with its subsequent re-foundings after the Civil War and (in part) after the Great Depression, reform of the economic order has, in every case, been central to their efforts to preserve self-government. Because Americans have always seen the fate of democracy as bound up with political economy.
